item.title: China extends suspension of new rare earth controls until January 10
item.description: Beijing extended the suspension of export controls on certain rare earths, industrial diamonds and lithium battery technology as it negotiates a broader trade deal with Washington ...
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: China on Monday announced a two-month extension of export-control waivers due to expire this month, preserving part of a wide-ranging deal struck after a summit between Presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump. China introduced export controls on certain rare earths in April 2025, only to expand them further in October of that year, dramatically widening their scope and also adding new controls on certain diamonds with industrial applications and lithium battery technology. The measures were then paused for one year last November after a summit in South Korea between Xi and Trump. The Ministry of Commerce said in a short statement on Monday that the pause would be extended for two months until January 10. It gave no other details. The extension is part of a broader suspension of trade countermeasures and tariffs announced by China on Monday as it negotiates with Washington over an enduring trade deal. Trump is set to travel to Shenzhen in southern China later this month for an APEC leaders summit, where he is expected to meet with Xi.

item.title: From Nvidia to Micron: Major China-linked espionage cases under scrutiny
item.description: From Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to Micron's semiconductor trade secrets, explore major cases of alleged Chinese honeytrapping, political influence and corporate espionage.
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / From Nvidia to Micron: Major China-linked espionage cases under scrutiny

From Nvidia to Micron: Major China-linked espionage cases under scrutiny Nvidia's probe into alleged Chinese intelligence targeting of CEO Jensen Huang puts the spotlight on past cases involving honeytrapping, political influence, trade secret theft and cyber espionage

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's case has brought renewed attention to concerns over corporate espionage and intelligence gathering. | Image: Bloomberg

Sarjna Rai New Delhi 5 min read Last Updated : Nov 09 2026 | 5:16 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Nvidia is investigating whether its Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang was targeted by Chinese intelligence through a personal relationship, bringing renewed attention to allegations of honeytrapping and corporate espionage.   According to The New York Times , United States (US) intelligence suspects that Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based chip company Megaspeed, was recruited by China's Ministry of State Security to cultivate a relationship with Huang and gather information about him. Meanwhile, Megaspeed has come under scrutiny over allegations that it helped Chinese entities access Nvidia AI chips restricted under US export controls. Huang has also acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife and apologised to his family and colleagues.

China has rejected the allegations, with Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun calling the claims of a Chinese spy plot against Huang "unsubstantiated" and a smear campaign against Beijing.   The allegations come amid intensifying competition between the US and China over artificial intelligence and semiconductor technology, where access to sensitive information and influential business networks can offer a significant strategic advantage.   What is honeytrapping?   Honeytrapping is an intelligence-gathering technique in which an individual uses romantic or intimate relationships to gain access to confidential information, influence decisions or compromise a target. Also Read

The person being targeted may be a government official, corporate executive, scientist or employee with access to sensitive information. Rather than relying on conventional surveillance, the operation uses emotional attachment, trust or the possibility of blackmail to achieve its objectives.

However, honeytrapping does not always involve stealing classified documents. It can also involve cultivating an influential relationship to shape business decisions, secure introductions or gain access to important networks.   While the Nvidia allegations have brought honeytrapping back into the spotlight, several other cases illustrate the different methods used to obtain sensitive information or cultivate political influence. Not all these cases involved proven honeytrapping operations.   Major China-linked honeytrapping and influence cases   1. Christine Fang, a Chinese national suspected by US intelligence of working for China's Ministry of State Security, allegedly cultivated relationships with American politicians to gain access to influential political circles.   According to an investigation by Axios , she built connections with local and national politicians through fundraising, networking and personal relationships. She reportedly had romantic relationships with at least two Midwestern mayors and developed links with then-Congressman Eric Swalwell.

The FBI reportedly alerted Swalwell to its concerns in 2015, after which he cut off contact with Fang.   2. Benjamin Bishop, a former US Army lieutenant colonel and civilian defence contractor at US Pacific Command, was sentenced to 87 months in prison in September 2014 for sharing classified military information allegedly with a 27-year-old Chinese woman with whom he was romantically involved.   The two reportedly met at a military-related conference in Hawaii. Bishop emailed her classified information concerning US military planning and joint operations with South Korea. He also removed classified documents from his workplace.   Bishop pleaded guilty to communicating classified national defence information to an unauthorised person and unlawfully retaining classified documents.

3. Another prominent case involving personal relationships dates back to 2003, when the FBI arrested Katrina Leung, a Chinese-American businesswoman accused of passing classified information to China.   According to the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), Leung had persuaded an FBI agent to share classified information with her over a period of 10 years, which she then passed to China. The case illustrated how personal relationships could be exploited to obtain sensitive intelligence.   4. A 2024 Financial Times report highlighted questions raised by French lawmakers over marriages between Chinese female students and sailors stationed at French naval bases in Brest. The relationships prompted concerns about possible intelligence-gathering activities, although they were not established as honeytrap operations.

As competition between countries increasingly extends to technology and commercial capabilities, companies have become targets for attempts to obtain proprietary research, trade secrets and technological expertise. Such activities fall under the broader practice of corporate espionage.   What is corporate espionage?   Corporate espionage involves the covert or illegal acquisition of confidential business information, intellectual property, trade secrets or technological expertise to gain a competitive or strategic advantage.   Unlike conventional industrial competition, it involves methods such as hacking, insider recruitment, employee poaching and unauthorised access to proprietary research.   Some notable cases with Chinese-links include:   1. In 2018, the US Department of Justice charged Chinese state-owned semiconductor company Fujian Jinhua, Taiwan-based United Microelectronics Corporation (UMC) and three individuals with conspiring to steal trade secrets from US chipmaker Micron Technology.

The former Micron employees downloaded confidential files containing information about the design and manufacture of dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) chips before moving to UMC. One employee reportedly downloaded more than 900 confidential files.   The alleged objective was to transfer Micron's technology to Jinhua, helping it develop advanced memory chips without years of independent research and development.   2. In May 2022, cybersecurity firm Cybereason reported that a Chinese state-linked hacking group, identified as APT41, had conducted a prolonged cyber espionage campaign against around 30 multinational companies.   Dubbed Operation CuckooBees, the campaign allegedly targeted businesses in the manufacturing, energy and pharmaceutical sectors across North America, Europe and Asia.

According to CBS News report, the hackers stole hundreds of gigabytes of sensitive information, including engineering blueprints, manufacturing designs, pharmaceutical research and proprietary formulas. The estimated value of the intellectual property stolen ran into trillions of dollars.   The scale of Chinese espionage is also reflected in a survey by the CSIS, which identified 224 publicly reported incidents targeting US since 2000. Of these, 54 per cent sought commercial technologies, while 46 per cent involved cyber espionage. The survey also highlighted the continued use of traditional recruitment methods, including intimate relationships and financial incentives, to obtain sensitive information.

item.content:encoded:
Home / Markets / News / Nvidia's shares slide as chip giant probes CEO Huang over spy claims

Nvidia's shares slide as chip giant probes CEO Huang over spy claims Nvidia's shares tumbled more than 6% in Frankfurt trading, extending last week's selloff and pushing the stock to fresh multi-month lows

Nvidia shares fell sharply on Monday. (Photo: Reuters)

Reuters 5 min read Last Updated : Nov 09 2026 | 2:42 PM IST

Nvidia shares fell sharply on Monday after an internal investigation into whether CEO Jensen Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort put his future at the AI chipmaker under scrutiny.   The internal probe ??followed a media report that Huang had a close relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who allegedly passed information to Beijing. Huang told Nvidia's employees that he had been unfaithful to his wife, without disclosing details of the relationship.   The investigation, announced on Sunday, has put a spotlight on Huang's future given Nvidia's status as the world's most valuable chipmaker and the CEO's role as the most prolific salesman of the AI boom.

The leather-jacketed Huang enjoys rock-star status worldwide, particularly in Asia, where he often mingles freely with fans, taking selfies and signing autographs for his devoted followers.   The fallout from the probe extended to South Korea, where Madison Huang, Huang's daughter and an Nvidia executive, cancelled a planned visit to Seoul for an Nvidia conference that was set to begin on Monday, according to companies she had been scheduled to meet.   Also Read

Nvidia CEO Huang probe: China calls 'spy narrative' unsubstantiated

Chinese newspaper dismisses Nvidia CEO Huang spy claim, warns on ties

Jensen Huang is bigger than Nvidia, and that spells trouble for AI

From Trump to Bill Ackman: Reactions to Nvidia's probe into CEO Huang

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair admission counters past statements on ties

Nvidia's shares tumbled more than 6% in Frankfurt trading, extending last week's selloff and pushing the stock to fresh multi-month lows. At those levels, the chipmaker stood to lose about $270 billion from its closing price on Friday, according to LSEG Datastream.

"The market's probably telling you now this does no favours to the stock whatsoever in a time when there's a lot of conjecture as to the build-out of data centres," said Chris Weston, head of research at brokerage Pepperstone in Melbourne. But Weston said he did not think Huang, whom he described as the "godfather of AI", would be replaced. "If we genuinely thought he was going to step down ... the stock would be down - it would be an absolute bloodbath, to be honest," he said.   The New York Times reported last month that Huang had a relationship with Alice Huang, an unrelated former executive of Singapore-based company Megaspeed, who US authorities investigated and concluded was a Chinese intelligence asset.

"The so-called Chinese spy narrative is purely a groundless accusation, slander, and a smear," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters in Beijing.   Megaspeed did not respond immediately to a request for comment on Monday, a public holiday in Singapore. Alice Huang did not respond to the New York Times last month when it first reported her relationship with Huang, and Reuters could not determine her location to seek comment on Monday.   ASIA PARTNERS UNAFFECTED   Shares in Nvidia's key Asian chip suppliers TSMC, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix rebounded on Monday after last week's selloff of AI-related stocks. TSMC shares jumped 6.5%, while those in Samsung and SK Hynix climbed 2.9% and 4.7%, respectively.

Some prominent figures weighed in on Huang's admission. Billionaire investor Bill Ackman, founder of Pershing Square Capital Management, said on X that the Nvidia CEO was an "incredible human," but if "indeed this is more than an affair, then it is obviously a real problem."   "I am hoping for a simple affair, not a risk to our national security," he added.   Tesla CEO Elon Musk commented, "I agree", on a post by Sequoia partner Shaun Maguire that said Huang "did something incredibly dumb" that was "bad ??for America" but that "Jensen is irreplaceable for America's AI leadership". US President Donald Trump said on Sunday he had not spoken to Huang about the allegations, but called him a fine person. "I hope everything's fine. He's done such an incredible job," he added.

When asked if he believed he should have acted on intelligence when he was briefed about it, Trump said: "No, I don't think so. I think he's an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it." The New York Times reported that Trump was briefed about the intelligence findings roughly a year ago and chose not to do anything with the information.   CANCELLED VISIT   Madison Huang had initially planned to visit South Korean AI startup Rebellions and hold a question-and-answer session with Kakao Mobility. Rebellions said the events were cancelled due to "unavoidable internal circumstances at Nvidia."

Nvidia AI Day Seoul, a two-day event expected to draw about 2,000 participants to discuss physical AI, agentic AI and infrastructure, will proceed as planned, according to South Korean media. Nvidia did not respond immediately to a request for comment.   Analysts said a prolonged investigation or internal review could potentially delay Nvidia's investment decisions or product launches, with broader implications for the semiconductor industry.   Ryu Young-ho, a senior analyst at NH Investment & Securities, said Nvidia's rivals, including Advanced Micro Devices, could attract greater attention in the short term, potentially putting Samsung, which has close business ties with AMD, in the spotlight.

Still, he said Nvidia's products would be difficult to replace, limiting the potential impact, although shipments to China could face further delays depending on how the situation developed.   South Korea's deputy science minister said on Monday the government expected no disruptions to contracted deliveries of Nvidia graphics processing units despite issues currently facing the company.   (Only the headline and picture of this report may have been reworked by the Business Standard staff; the rest of the content is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)   More From This Section

item.content:encoded:
Home / Technology / Tech News / Bill Gates says billionaires should pay more taxes as AI reshapes economy

Bill Gates says billionaires should pay more taxes as AI reshapes economy Gates said that governments must take primary responsibility for tackling inequality as AI generates wealth, warning that philanthropy cannot replace public support systems

Gates also highlighted the need to reconsider how governments tax labour and capital as businesses increasingly adopt AI tools and automation | Image: Bloomberg

Apexa Rai New Delhi 2 min read Last Updated : Nov 09 2026 | 1:49 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates has called for governments to reconsider taxation policies and ensure that billionaires and wealthy individuals contribute more towards addressing inequality, as the rapid growth of artificial intelligence(AI) threatens to widen the gap between rich and poor.   Speaking on the Financial Times' Tech Tonic podcast, Gates said governments must take primary responsibility for tackling economic inequality, rather than relying on charitable contributions from wealthy individuals.   "The primary responsibility of dealing with inequality will always rest with governments. We can't expect philanthropy, which is voluntary in nature, to be the safety net," Gates said.   He argued that tax systems would need to adapt to an economy increasingly shaped by AI , including ensuring that people with substantial wealth and billionaires contribute towards public welfare.

The comments come amid growing concerns that the economic gains from AI could remain concentrated among technology companies, investors and wealthy individuals, even as automation changes the nature of employment across industries. Also Read

Gates also highlighted the need to reconsider how governments tax labour and capital as businesses increasingly adopt AI tools and automation. Existing tax structures, he said, can make investment in machines more financially attractive than employing people.   In an essay published on his website, Gates Notes, he had previously proposed taxing robots, arguing that automation could otherwise accelerate job displacement without generating equivalent contributions towards public finances.   The Microsoft co-founder believes governments could use tax revenues to support workers affected by technological changes.

Gates, who has pledged to give away virtually all his wealth through the Gates Foundation over the next two decades, maintains that charitable giving cannot substitute for government-funded welfare and public services.
